name: Jamal Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a haul truck from the cut to the sorting area at the large mine. I've got a vocational certificate and enough years in the seat to know when a loaded truck needs a longer stopping distance, but my pay is below what this work usually brings. My partner Noor works part-time at a bakery; our children are grown and live elsewhere. We spent our savings on dental treatment and now have less than a month of bills put aside. There are few other equipment jobs near our town; I use an AI tool now and then to make sense of a maintenance notice, after the workshop has approved the notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little AI filling forms is all right if the truck inspection still belongs to the driver. A neat report doesn't tell me whether a brake pedal feels soft on the descent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My driving hours probably stay in this mild picture, but Noor's bakery shifts vary and our savings are thin after the dental bill. The mine's lower rate leaves us little to rebuild with even if nothing radical changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the brake check at the start of each run and record any odd feel in the workshop book. This month Noor and I would work out the minimum we need from both pay packets, then I'd ask the supervisor how my rate is set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a bit stretched already. Small AI is not the worry; another week of short bakery shifts would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the supervisor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to see the operator scale and where my certificate places me. I don't need a grand speech, just the reason my hourly rate is what it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the dental bill keep recurring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The treatment is paid for, but it used the money we kept for surprises. We are not paying for grown children's school fees now, yet rebuilding a cushion on this wage is slow.

say: I would keep **truck inspection** with the driver.
I would ask how the mine sets my **hourly rate**.
think: My driving hours look steady, but our **cushion** is gone.
Noor’s changing bakery shifts make **household income** uncertain.
do: Continue the **brake check** and record concerns for the workshop.
Calculate minimum household pay and ask about the **operator scale**.
feel: I feel **stretched** by income variation even in a mild scenario.
S0.quote: A neat report doesn't tell me whether a brake pedal feels soft on the descent.
fieldNote: His **dental expense** depleted savings, while variable bakery shifts keep pressure on the household.
He uses AI occasionally for **approved notices** but anchors his work in physical vehicle checks.

steps.text: Keep checking haul-truck brakes and logging unusual pedal feel
Ask the supervisor how his certificate affects operator pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that better planning could reduce waiting at the sorter, but we need to know whether that means fewer driving shifts. If another operator has tested the new dispatch display, I would give it a try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My truck is hands-on work, yet an AI schedule could cut paid waiting time or combine runs. Few nearby mines are hiring, and Noor's bakery income would not cover our rent if my shifts dropped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for three months of trip and paid-hour records and compare them with the proposed dispatch schedule. In the first year I'd try the approved display beside an experienced driver, and if hours fell I'd ask the local freight yard about equipment vacancies and drop our paid sports subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but I can check the numbers. I would rather argue from our actual hours than from a rumour about software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which driver would you sit with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mina, who has used the display on the night shift. She will tell me if it sends a truck around a bend that has been closed for repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the freight yard take you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know whether its equipment is close enough to what I drive now. I'd ask about a trial and the required licence before assuming that job is mine.

say: I would ask if faster dispatch means fewer **paid shifts**.
I would try a **tested display** with an experienced driver.
think: AI scheduling could reduce my **paid hours** before robots arrive.
Noor’s bakery wage cannot cover our **rent** alone.
do: Compare three months of **trip records** with the new schedule.
Try approved dispatch with Mina and ask the **freight yard** about vacancies if hours fall.
feel: I feel **anxious**, yet able to check actual hours.
S1.quote: I would rather argue from our actual hours than from a rumour about software.
fieldNote: He accepts **proven dispatch tools** after a trusted operator tests them on real mine roads.
His **freight-yard inquiry** is exploratory because he has not confirmed equipment fit or licensing.

steps.text: Compare three months of paid haul hours with the proposed schedule
Try the approved dispatch display with experienced driver Mina
Ask the freight yard about vacancies if mine hours fall
Cancel the sports subscription if truck hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 will rewrite dispatch and robots that can drive trucks come around 2031. I want the mine to publish the purchase timetable and the paid jobs it thinks drivers can move into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the autonomous trucks to take a large share of our shifts, including mine, by the robot date. At 60 and then 63 I cannot make a month of bills stretch out of savings we no longer have, and I wake early thinking about the rent if both our wages run short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor now for the equipment timetable and take our pay records to an employment adviser. If truck hours fell in 2028, I'd ask the freight yard about a paid equipment assessment and keep every safe mine shift in 2029; I'd enroll in a funded road-vehicle licence course only if the yard confirmed it needed that licence for a posted job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the speed. I can learn a new display, but a display skill will not create a replacement wage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Noor after the early waking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Noor I have been counting the rent against her bakery rota before dawn. We would put the figures on paper and decide who to call first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a road-vehicle licence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A mine haul truck is not the same as a road lorry. If the freight yard has paid driving work, I need to know its licence rule before spending time on a course.

say: I would request a **purchase timetable** and posted paid roles.
I would explain that **2028 dispatch** changes precede truck robots around 2031.
think: I expect a large loss of **truck shifts** by 2031.
Our thin savings and variable bakery wage expose the **rent**.
do: Ask for the mine’s **equipment timetable** and meet an employment adviser.
Seek a yard assessment and take **funded licence training** only if a posted job requires it.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and wake early worrying about rent.
S2.quote: A mine haul truck is not the same as a road lorry.
fieldNote: He expects significant **shift loss** at the robot date and describes early waking over rent.
A **licence course** requires funding and a real vacancy requiring the credential.

steps.text: Ask the mine for a written autonomous-truck purchase timetable
Meet an employment adviser with household pay records
Ask the freight yard for a paid equipment assessment if mine hours fall
Enroll in funded road-vehicle licence training if a posted yard job requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends that thinking AI in 2031 and truck robots around 2034 give the mine a few years to train current drivers. I would want one tested route and a clear rule about who steps in when a truck stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 at the thinking date and 66 when robots arrive. Retirement might sound near, but with less than a month saved today I cannot plan to leave paid work just because a truck can drive itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking haul shifts and ask Mina to show me the approved fleet display after it has worked safely for a while. In 2032 I'd apply for a paid equipment post at the freight yard if one appears; after robots arrive I'd seek the mine's vehicle-recovery work if it posts positions and I can qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed than in the fast picture. I still worry about how we will pay rent, but a few years lets me test a real tool and check an actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retrain for vehicle recovery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid practical course if the mine offered one and showed us the job description. I don't want to pretend that knowing a display makes me fit to recover a heavy truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the fleet display fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write down the location and stop the vehicle according to the mine rule. A trial is useful only when people can report faults without being called difficult.

say: I would ask for a **tested route** and a clear stop rule.
I would put capable truck robots around **2034**.
think: Retirement at **66** remains uncertain with our thin savings.
I may need a paid **recovery role** if driving seats shrink.
do: Keep **haul shifts** and test the fleet display with Mina after it proves safe.
Apply for **freight-yard work** if posted and take paid recovery training if offered.
feel: I feel **less rushed**, though rent still needs a wage.
S3.quote: A trial is useful only when people can report faults without being called difficult.
fieldNote: His **measured adoption** depends on field proof and a fault-reporting rule.
He separates a possible **recovery vacancy** from an assured job and keeps paid work central.

steps.text: Try the approved fleet display with Mina after a safe field trial
Apply for paid equipment work at the freight yard if posted
Take paid vehicle-recovery training if the mine offers a real post
Keep taking safe paid haul-truck shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2036 and truck robots around 2039 leave time to deal honestly with drivers. I would still ask the mine for pay and retirement figures now, because a decade does not settle a household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 at the first date and 71 when robots can drive. I may have stopped night trips by then, but I cannot count on full retirement while our reserve is this small and the rent keeps coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving as long as my eyesight and reactions remain sound, and Noor and I would review the budget every year. In 2037 I'd compare our actual retirement income with rent before cutting hours; if it failed, I'd ask the freight yard about paid work and continue safe mine shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the present money more than the distant robot. We have time to make choices, but only if we can afford to keep a little of each pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save out of current wages?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set aside a small amount in months when the bakery and mine both pay full hours. In a short month I would pay rent first and not pretend a transfer to savings happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have their own households. I would ask them for help understanding a form, but not make their wages part of our retirement plan.

say: I would ask for current **pay and retirement figures**.
I would place truck robots around **2039**, after thinking AI.
think: I may stop night trips by **71**, but retirement is uncertain.
The present **rent bill** matters more than a distant machine.
do: Keep safe **driving shifts** and review the household budget annually.
Compare real income with **rent** in 2037 before reducing hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about current money despite the long timeline.
S4.quote: In a short month I would pay rent first and not pretend a transfer to savings happened.
fieldNote: His **thin reserve** keeps the distant scenario financially anxious despite a possible retirement window.
**Saving** requires full hours in both household jobs, and he prioritises rent in short months.

steps.text: Keep driving mine haul trucks while eyesight and reactions remain safe
Set aside pay in months when both jobs provide full hours
Ask the freight yard for paid work if 2037 retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a truck could be ordered before I have time to replace the wage it takes. A published timetable, paid practical training for a posted job and honest pay figures would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the new truck can stop safely on the wet descent. A fleet report looks clean until a driver has to trust the brakes on that slope.

headlineQuote: A fleet report looks clean until a driver has to trust the brakes on that slope.
portrait: Jamal is an **experienced haul-truck driver** at a large mine, earning below the usual rate.
He and Noor have grown children and less than **one month** saved after dental treatment.
He uses AI **occasionally** and tries proven mine tools with another driver.
He checks **pay records**, freight-yard vacancies and funded credentials before changing jobs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because truck automation could remove wages before he finds local work.
whatWouldHelp: A published **purchase timetable**, paid training linked to a vacancy and honest pay figures would help.
